about: A body's shape from its spin (and, later, a companion's pull): XO design, 'shape from spin and a companion's pull for every body'. The tidal part (sse.shape.spin_and_pull, Roche model) will take this block's output.

checks.says: mass must be more than zero, got {}
radius must be more than zero, got {}
rotation period must be a number, got {}
the moment of inertia factor lies between 0 (all mass at the centre) and 0.4 (uniform), got {}

references: Radau, R. 1885 and Darwin, G. H. 1899, the Darwin-Radau relation between flattening and the moment of inertia of a body in hydrostatic equilibrium; as given in Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press, eq. 4.48 and 4.49. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817
Hubbard, W. B. 1984, Planetary Interiors, Van Nostrand Reinhold (q = ω²R³/GM and first-order flattening)
atoms.shown: q = ω²R_eq³/GM, ω = 2π/P; f = (5/2) q / (1 + (25/4)(1 − (3/2)C)²); R_eq = R (1 − f)^(−1/3) (one step from the mean radius), R_pol = R_eq (1 − f)

equation.name: How much a spinning world bulges at its equator
equation.formula:
w = 2 * pi / abs(P)
d = 1 - 3 / 2 * C
k = 5 / 2 / (1 + 25 / 4 * d * d)
q0 = w * w * R * R * R / (G * M)
R1 = R / cbrt(1 - k * q0)
q = w * w * R1 * R1 * R1 / (G * M)
f = k * q
Re = R / cbrt(1 - f)
Rp = Re * (1 - f)

R.name: mean radius of the world (a sphere of the same volume)

P.name: time for one turn (negative when it turns backwards)

C.name: moment of inertia over M R² (0.4 uniform, lower when mass sinks to the centre)

f.name: flattening: how much shorter the pole-to-pole radius is, as a share of the equator's

q.name: spin's pull outward at the equator over gravity's pull in

source.text: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics

explain.curious: A world that spins fast flings its equator outward, so it bulges; Saturn spins in under 11 hours and is a tenth wider than it is tall.
explain.science: Hydrostatic flattening to first order from the spin parameter q (with the equatorial radius, found in one step from the mean radius) and the moment of inertia factor C (Darwin-Radau). Within about a percent for the giants and Earth; very fast spinners (q above about 0.3) need the Maclaurin sequence.
